newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Joint legalisation push at UK cannabis conference. [CORRECTED 22:55 GMT 20/10]
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Joint legalisation push at UK cannabis conference. [CORRECTED 22:55 GMT 20/10]

text.p: Mick Marlow, imprisoned for writing a book on cultivating marijuana, spent his first full day of freedom in a dilapidated London cinema lobbying for legislation of the drug.

The "Annual Conference on Cannabis" brought together several hundred enthusiasts, both professional and amateur, who smoked and inhaled throughout a day celebrating cannabis and its many uses in industry, food, medicine and, of course, relaxation.
Veggie burgers containing hemp seeds, clothing made of hemp and smoking paraphernalia were on sale.
Raw and roasted marijuana seeds -- legal as long as they aren't germinated -- were available for sampling. Raffle tickets offered the chance to win a five-foot (1.60 metre) tall waterpipe.
A few said they came to the conference to pick up tips on growing, but most said they came to show support for the cause of legalisation and to get high with friends.
And there wasn't a policeman in sight.
Cannabis possession remains illegal in Britain and growing it can attract heavy prison sentences. The question of legalisation was on everyone lips, along with hefty joints.

Briton Howard Marks, recently released from a seven-year jail term in the United States for drug smuggling, told the meeting the quality of pot had deteriorated because today's smugglers aren't users.
Marks wants to see high-quality marijuana sold legally in police stations, chemists and "head" shops across Britain.
Dutchman Wernard (he prefers not to use his last name) advocated a system not unlike that in the Netherlands where marijuana is illegal but tolerated in small quantities.
Legalising cannabis, Wernard said, would commercialise the product just like tobacco. "It shouldn't be in the hands of those who don't smoke it," he declared.

Wernard dreams of creating a "cannabis culture", in which every user grows no more than eight marijuana plants for their own consumption.Marlow had no plants in jail but said he managed to smoke the weed at least twice a week nonetheless.
Robin Scott, a clean-cut Oxford graduate, extolled the virtues of marijuana's medical properties. (Corrects to make clear that Scott is not an ordained minister of the Church of Scientology)
Scott and his wife founded the Medical Marijuana Foundation and were developing a marijuana "vitamin" until they got busted.

Scott reckons cannabis will be legal in Britain within a year. "If it doesn't happen this year, it's bound to happen next year," he said. "It's like the Berlin Wall. People are not going to live with these restrictions any longer."
Marks told the crowd he would consider becoming a candidate for Britain's Cannabis Party if it remained committed to the single issue of legalising marijuana.

The Cannabis Party plans to put up a handful of candidates at the next general election to push its legalisation campaign. "The need to get political is paramount," one party member told the gathering. "Go out and tell everyone that cannabis is not a drug, it's a relaxant, and we need to legalise it."
The conference was organised by Rob Christopher, a former civil engineer, who paid for the hire of the cinema with money he inherited.
"At least I'm doing something constructive with it," Christopher said. "My grandfather was a successful drug dealer -- an alcohol dealer. I have a lot of karma to pay back."
He founded the Cannabis Hemp Information Club a year ago, Unlike alcohol, cannabis has not been shown to promote aggressive or violent behaviour, he said.
"If everyone smoked cannabis, we'd live in a much more chilled-out society," Christopher added.

Christopher said he plans to open a distribution centre in London. He will give cannabis to anyone who intends to use it for medicinal purposes as the government would not recognise its medical benefits.
"The government has been lying to us," he said. "The government won't give us the best medicine.
"This plant can actually reverse the effects of global warming, save the deforestation of rain forests, and provide food, fuel and medicine to millions of people," he added.
Christopher says he hasn't smoked the stuff himself for a while. If he had, he never would have been able to organise the conference.
"If I was getting stoned, I would have just sat back and said, "no worries, someone else will do it'," he said.
